Slovakia’s Tourism Industry Faces Widespread Disruption as Workers Walk Out

Bratislava – Slovakia’s tourism sector has come to a standstill as thousands of workers staged a coordinated walkout on Tuesday, demanding improved wages and better working conditions. The strike, organized by the Slovak Tourism Workers’ Union (STWU), began at 6 a.m. and continued into Wednesday, severely affecting operations at major attractions, tour operators, and visitor information centers across the country.

The walkout has impacted popular sites such as the Bratislava Castle, the High Tatras National Park, and the UNESCO-listed town of Banská Štiavnica, where tours and guided experiences were suspended. Several hotels and resorts under the nationwide chain Slovenské Zážitky reported that their guest services, including guided excursions and ticketing desks, remained closed throughout the day. According to the STWU, roughly 70% of the industry’s workforce participated in the strike, leaving only skeletal crews to handle basic visitor inquiries.

“We have reached a breaking point,” said Ivana Malinová, chair of the STWU. “For too long, tourism workers have faced low pay and seasonal insecurity, even as visitor numbers have rebounded to pre-pandemic levels. Our members deserve fair compensation for the vital role they play in Slovakia’s tourism success.”

Industry association SlovakTourism estimated that ticket sales at major sites dropped between 60% and 90% compared to an average weekday in June. “The loss of guided tours has been particularly damaging,” said Andrej Kováč, the association’s spokesperson. “Many visitors are left without access to essential services that enhance their experience and understanding of our heritage.”

The Ministry of Tourism has called for urgent talks between union representatives and management from firms such as Karpatské Dobrodružstvá and Tatry Explorers. “We are monitoring the situation closely and urge all parties to return to negotiations,” said Deputy Minister Jozef Šimek in a statement.

As the walkout entered its second day, union leaders signaled that the strike would continue until concrete commitments are made. “Our members are united and determined,” Malinová said. “We call on employers to recognize the value of our work.”
